lessons.title: Selection of Healthy Broodstock
lessons.body:
Selecting healthy broodstock is the first step to producing quality fingerlings. Start by choosing fish that are 8â12 months old for tilapia and 6â10 months for catfish, as these ages give good egg and sperm quality. Look for fish with a body weight of at least 200â300 g for tilapia and 500â800 g for catfish. Avoid fish that are too fat or too thin; a healthy broodfish has a rounded belly and a thick base to the tail.

Examine each fish closely. The eyes should be clear and bright, not cloudy. The skin should be smooth, shiny, and free of wounds, spots, or parasites. The fins should be intact, not ragged or bloody. Gills should be bright red, not pale or brown. Check the vent (the opening near the tail) â it should be clean and slightly pink, not red or swollen. Any fish showing signs of disease, deformity, or slow movement should be removed immediately.

Source your broodstock from a reputable hatchery or from your own best-performing ponds. Never mix fish from different farms without quarantine, as this spreads diseases. In Africa, many farmers use Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) or African catfish (Clarias gariepinus). For tilapia, select fish that are 6â8 months old and 150â250 g; for catfish, 8â12 months and 800â1200 g. Always choose more females than males, usually 2â3 females for every male.

Before stocking, weigh and measure each fish. Record the data in a notebook. A good broodfish should gain weight steadily. If you are buying from a hatchery, ask for health certificates and check for common diseases like tilapia lake virus or catfish iridovirus. Quarantine new fish in a separate tank for 14 days, treating with salt (3â5 g per litre) to reduce stress and kill external parasites.

Finally, handle fish gently with wet hands or a soft net. Rough handling causes stress, which lowers egg quality. Keep broodstock in clean, well-aerated water with a temperature of 26â30Â°C and a pH of 6.5â8.5. A simple test kit for ammonia, nitrite, and pH is essential. By selecting only the best fish, you set the foundation for strong, fast-growing fingerlings.

lessons.title: Broodstock Nutrition and Feeding Regimes
lessons.body:
Proper nutrition is critical for broodstock because it directly affects egg quality, sperm count, and the health of the fry. Broodfish need a diet with 35â40% protein, 6â8% fat, and added vitamins and minerals. You can use commercial broodstock pellets, but many African farmers make their own mix. A simple recipe: 40% fishmeal, 30% soybean meal, 20% maize or wheat bran, 5% cassava flour, and 5% vitamin-mineral premix. Add 2% cod liver oil or vegetable oil for essential fatty acids.

Feed broodfish twice a day, at 8â9 am and 4â5 pm. Give them 2â3% of their total body weight per day. For example, if you have 10 kg of broodfish, feed 200â300 g of feed daily. Adjust the amount based on water temperature: in warm months (28â30Â°C), feed more; in cool months (below 24Â°C), reduce to 1% body weight. Overfeeding causes fat deposits that reduce fertility; underfeeding leads to small, weak eggs.

Supplement with natural foods. In ponds, broodfish will eat algae, insects, and small crustaceans. You can also add chopped earthworms, termites, or small fish once a week. For tilapia, add 10â20% of feed as spirulina or chlorella to boost colour and egg quality. For catfish, add 5% squid meal or shrimp meal. Always store feed in a cool, dry place and use within 3 months to prevent mould.

Water quality affects feeding. Keep dissolved oxygen above 5 mg/L and ammonia below 0.5 mg/L. If fish gasp at the surface, stop feeding and increase aeration. Use a simple aeration pump or splash water. During spawning season, increase protein to 40% and add 1% garlic powder to stimulate appetite and prevent disease.

Record feed amounts daily. A 100 g female tilapia should gain 2â3 g per week. If she is not gaining, check for disease or poor water quality. For catfish, a 1 kg female should gain 5â10 g per week. Adjust feed based on condition â you should be able to feel a slight fat layer but not a thick belly. Always remove uneaten feed after 30 minutes to avoid fouling the water. Healthy, well-fed broodstock produce 20â30% more eggs than poorly fed ones.

lessons.title: Broodstock Conditioning and Spawning Induction
lessons.body:
Conditioning prepares broodfish for spawning. Start 4â6 weeks before you want eggs. Move selected males and females to separate conditioning tanks. Use clean, well-aerated water at 28â30Â°C for tilapia and 26â28Â°C for catfish. Keep pH at 6.5â8.0 and ammonia below 0.1 mg/L. Feed a high-protein diet (40% protein) twice daily. For tilapia, condition at a density of 5â10 fish per cubic metre; for catfish, 3â5 fish per cubic metre.

For natural spawning, tilapia can be conditioned in harem tanks with one male to three females. Provide nesting sites like flat stones or plastic trays. After 2â3 weeks, females will show a swollen genital papilla and males will dig nests. For catfish, natural spawning is harder; you usually need hormone injection. Use a synthetic hormone like Ovaprim or human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG). For catfish, inject females with 0.5 ml Ovaprim per kg body weight, and males with half that dose. Inject into the muscle near the dorsal fin using a 1 ml syringe.

After injection, place one male and one female in a spawning tank with a substrate (like a piece of net or banana leaves) for catfish to lay eggs on. Keep water at 26â28Â°C and aerate gently. Eggs are released 10â12 hours after injection. For tilapia, you can also use hormonal induction if you want synchronized spawning. Use 17Î±-methyltestosterone? No, that is for sex reversal. For spawning, use HCG at 1000 IU per kg for females.

Monitor fish closely. Remove eggs after spawning to prevent parents from eating them. For tilapia, females mouthbrood eggs for 14â21 days. You can strip eggs from the female's mouth after 3â4 days and incubate them artificially in a hatchery jar. For catfish, eggs hatch in 24â36 hours at 28Â°C. Keep water clean and free of fungus by adding methylene blue at 2 mg/L.

Record all dates, hormone doses, and water temperatures. A simple notebook works. After spawning, return broodfish to conditioning tanks and feed them well. They can be used again after 4â6 weeks. Always have backup males and females in case some do not respond.

lessons.title: Genetic Improvement and Selective Breeding
lessons.body:
Genetic improvement means choosing the best fish to breed so that future generations grow faster, resist disease, and taste better. Without selection, fish become stunted and weak after a few generations. Start by tagging or marking your best fish. Use small plastic tags or fin clips. Record growth rate, body shape, and survival. Select only fish that reach 200 g in 4 months (for tilapia) or 500 g in 6 months (for catfish).

Choose a minimum of 50 males and 150 females as your breeding population. Never breed brother to sister; that causes inbreeding and deformities. Instead, use a rotational system: divide your broodstock into 3â4 families. Each year, breed males from family A with females from family B, then B with C, and so on. This keeps genetic diversity high. In Africa, many farmers use the GIFT strain of Nile tilapia, which grows 30% faster than local strains.

Select for specific traits. For growth, weigh each fish at 4 and 8 months. Keep only the top 20% by weight. For disease resistance, expose fish to a mild disease challenge (like Streptococcus) and keep survivors. For body shape, choose fish with a deep body and small head. For colour, if you want red tilapia, select only red or pink fish. Always record data in a logbook: tag number, weight, length, date, and family.

Manage your breeding stock carefully. Keep each family in a separate tank or hap (a net cage). When they are ready to spawn, mix males and females from different families. After spawning, return them to their family tanks. Replace broodfish every 12â18 months to avoid old, poor-quality eggs. A good selective breeding programme can increase growth by 10â15% per generation.

Avoid common mistakes: do not select only the largest fish if they are sick or deformed. Do not use too few breeders. Do not mix strains without a plan. Work with other farmers to exchange males every 2 years. Simple records and consistent selection will give you a big advantage. Many African hatcheries now sell improved strains; buy from them if you cannot run your own programme.

lessons.title: Health Management of Broodstock
lessons.body:
Broodstock are valuable, so disease can be costly. Prevent problems by keeping water clean. Test water daily for temperature (26â30Â°C), pH (6.5â8.5), ammonia (0â0.5 mg/L), and nitrite (0â0.1 mg/L). Use a simple test kit. Change 20â30% of water every 2â3 days. Keep a separate quarantine tank for new fish. Quarantine for 14 days and treat with salt (3â5 g/L) or potassium permanganate (2 mg/L) for 30 minutes.

Common diseases in African broodstock include bacterial infections (Aeromonas, Streptococcus), fungal infections (Saprolegnia), and parasites (Trichodina, Ichthyophthirius). Signs: white spots, frayed fins, red ulcers, cloudy eyes, or rubbing against walls. For bacterial infections, use oxytetracycline at 50 mg/kg fish for 7 days in feed. For fungus, use methylene blue at 2â3 mg/L as a bath for 3 days. For parasites, use formalin at 25 ml per 1000 L for 1 hour, or salt baths (10 g/L for 30 minutes).

Vaccination is possible for some diseases. In Africa, vaccines for Streptococcus in tilapia are available. Vaccinate fish at 10â15 g size by injection. Keep records of vaccination dates. Also, use probiotics in feed (1 g/kg) to boost immunity. Add garlic (5 g/kg feed) and vitamin C (500 mg/kg feed) during stressful periods like spawning.

Handle fish gently to avoid stress. Stress lowers immunity. Do not overcrowd. Keep density at 5â10 kg per cubic metre for tilapia, 3â5 kg for catfish. Remove dead fish immediately. Disinfect nets and tanks with chlorine (10 mg/L) between uses. If disease occurs, isolate affected fish and treat the whole tank. Do not use antibiotics without veterinary advice; misuse causes resistance.

Record all treatments, dates, and doses. A healthy broodstock programme includes regular health checks every 2 weeks. Look at gills, skin, and fins under a magnifying glass. If you see problems, act fast. A sick broodfish produces poor eggs or none at all. By keeping your broodstock healthy, you ensure a steady supply of quality fingerlings.

lessons.title: Record Keeping and Broodstock Performance Evaluation
lessons.body:
Record keeping is the backbone of good broodstock management. Without records, you cannot tell which fish perform best. Use a simple notebook or a spreadsheet on a phone. For each broodfish, record: tag number, species, sex, date of birth, weight every month, length, feed amount, spawning dates, number of eggs, hatch rate, and any treatments. Also record water quality daily: temperature, pH, ammonia, and nitrite.

At spawning, record the male and female tag numbers, date, hormone dose (if used), time of spawning, number of eggs, and number of fry hatched. Calculate hatch rate: (number of fry / number of eggs) Ã 100. A good hatch rate for tilapia is 70â80%; for catfish, 60â70%. Calculate fecundity: number of eggs per gram of female body weight. For tilapia, expect 2â4 eggs per gram; for catfish, 10â20 eggs per gram.

Evaluate performance every 3 months. For each female, calculate average eggs per spawn, average hatch rate, and survival of fry to 30 days. For each male, check fertility by looking at egg hatch rate. Cull any female that produces less than 1 egg per gram or has hatch rate below 50%. Cull any male that sires eggs with hatch rate below 50%. Replace them with better fish from your selection programme.

Use a simple scoring system. Give each fish a score: growth (1â5), survival (1â5), and egg quality (1â5). Total score out of 15. Keep only fish scoring 10 or above. Record all scores. This helps you decide which fish to breed next season. Also track feed cost per fry produced. If feed cost is high, adjust feeding or cull poor performers.

Share records with other farmers or extension officers. They can help you spot trends. For example, if hatch rate drops in the dry season, you may need to adjust water temperature or feeding. Keep records for at least 2 years. This data is your best tool for improving your hatchery. A farmer who keeps good records can double production in 2â3 years. Start simple: a notebook and a pen. Then move to a phone app like Excel or Kobo Collect. The key is consistency.

quiz.q: What is the recommended age range for selecting tilapia broodstock?
quiz.explanation: Tilapia broodstock are best selected at 8â12 months for good egg and sperm quality.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a healthy broodfish?
quiz.explanation: Bright red gills indicate good health, while cloudy eyes and ragged fins are signs of disease.

quiz.q: How many females per male are recommended for tilapia broodstock?
quiz.explanation: A ratio of 2â3 females per male is standard for tilapia to ensure good spawning without stressing males.

quiz.q: What is the recommended quarantine period for new broodstock?
quiz.explanation: A 14-day quarantine helps prevent the spread of diseases to existing stock.

quiz.q: What protein level is recommended for broodstock feed?
quiz.explanation: Broodstock need 35â40% protein for good egg and sperm production.

quiz.q: How often should you feed broodfish?
quiz.explanation: Feeding twice a day at 2â3% body weight is ideal for broodstock.

quiz.q: What percentage of body weight should you feed broodfish daily?
quiz.explanation: Feeding 2â3% of body weight per day maintains good condition without overfeeding.

quiz.q: Which supplement can boost egg quality in tilapia?
quiz.explanation: Spirulina is rich in nutrients that improve egg quality and colour in tilapia.

quiz.q: What is the recommended conditioning period before spawning?
quiz.explanation: A 4â6 week conditioning period allows broodfish to develop good eggs and sperm.

quiz.q: Which hormone is commonly used to induce spawning in catfish?
quiz.explanation: Ovaprim is a synthetic hormone widely used for spawning induction in catfish.

quiz.q: How long after injection do catfish usually spawn?
quiz.explanation: Catfish typically spawn 10â12 hours after hormone injection at 26â28Â°C.

quiz.q: What is the recommended water temperature for conditioning tilapia broodstock?
quiz.explanation: Tilapia broodstock condition best at 28â30Â°C.

quiz.q: Why is inbreeding avoided in selective breeding?
options: B) It causes deformities and weak fish
quiz.explanation: Inbreeding leads to deformities, poor growth, and reduced disease resistance.

quiz.q: What is the minimum number of females recommended for a breeding population?
quiz.explanation: At least 150 females maintain genetic diversity and reduce inbreeding.

quiz.q: Which trait is commonly selected for in tilapia breeding programmes?
quiz.explanation: Fast growth is a key trait for improving productivity in tilapia.

quiz.q: How often should broodfish be replaced in a selective breeding programme?
quiz.explanation: Replacing broodfish every 12â18 months prevents decline in egg quality.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of bacterial infection in broodstock?
quiz.explanation: Red ulcers are a typical sign of bacterial infections like Aeromonas.

quiz.q: Which chemical is used to treat fungal infections in broodstock?
quiz.explanation: Methylene blue at 2â3 mg/L is effective against fungal infections.

quiz.q: What is the recommended salt concentration for a quarantine bath?
quiz.explanation: A salt bath of 3â5 g/L reduces stress and kills external parasites during quarantine.

quiz.q: How often should you check water quality in broodstock tanks?
quiz.explanation: Daily water quality checks help prevent disease and stress.

quiz.q: What is the recommended stocking density for tilapia broodstock?
quiz.explanation: 5â10 kg/mÂ³ is ideal for tilapia broodstock to reduce stress and disease.

quiz.q: Which record is essential for evaluating broodstock performance?
options: B) Number of eggs per spawn
quiz.explanation: Number of eggs per spawn directly measures reproductive performance.

quiz.q: What is a good hatch rate for tilapia eggs?
quiz.explanation: A hatch rate of 70â80% is considered good for tilapia.

quiz.q: How is fecundity calculated?
options: A) Number of eggs per female
B) Number of eggs per gram of female body weight
C) Number of fry per male
D) Number of spawns per year
quiz.explanation: Fecundity is the number of eggs per gram of female body weight.

quiz.q: What should you do with a female that produces less than 1 egg per gram?
quiz.explanation: Culling poor performers improves the overall quality of the broodstock.

quiz.q: How often should you evaluate broodstock performance?
quiz.explanation: Evaluating every 3 months allows timely culling and selection decisions.

quiz.q: What is a simple scoring system for broodstock?
quiz.explanation: A 1â5 scale for growth, survival, and egg quality is easy to use.

quiz.q: Why is record keeping important in broodstock management?
options: A) It helps identify best performers
quiz.explanation: Records help identify top-performing fish for selective breeding.

quiz.q: What is the recommended minimum score to keep a broodfish?
quiz.explanation: Keeping fish that score 10 or above ensures good overall performance.

quiz.q: How long should broodstock records be kept?
quiz.explanation: Keeping records for at least 2 years helps track trends and improve management.
